title: Mosques of mud and wood
hook: Djenné in Mali, wooden mosques in China and Java

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Aqsa, the Far Distant Place of Worship in Jerusalem. Your line was the farthest mosque. When the city came up, did you pause and wish it peace? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Three roofs. The first is flat, on walls of sun-dried mud bristling with wooden poles, in Djenné, in Mali. The second curves up at the corners like a temple roof, painted beams under clay tiles, in a courtyard in China. The third is stacked in layers, roof on roof on roof, a tall wooden pyramid in Java, in Indonesia. No dome on any of them. No tall pencil minaret. And all three are mosques, where people line up in rows and bow toward Mecca. How can three buildings look so unlike each other and do the same thing? Today: mosques of mud and wood.
screen: `A ROOF OF MUD IN MALI.` → `A TEMPLE ROOF IN CHINA.` → `A STACKED ROOF IN JAVA.`

segments.voice: The answer starts with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he counts the things given to him, and one of them is this: the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him and his community. Wherever the time of prayer finds you, you can pray there. So a mosque, at its simplest, is a clean place set apart, with the direction of Mecca marked. Everything else, the walls, the roof, the shape, is left to the builders. And builders use what they have. Second, the mud. We met Djenné earlier this year, the town that replasters its mosque together. Look this time at the method. In a land of river clay and heat, thick mud walls help keep a building cool, and the wooden poles in them give the plasterers a foothold when the walls are renewed. The material is local; so is the work. Third, the wood in China. Some old Chinese mosques were built in the style of Chinese halls: courtyards, gates, timber halls, curved roofs, inscriptions in Arabic and in Chinese characters side by side. A visitor might take one for a temple until the rows begin. Fourth, Java. Some of the old mosques there have tiered roofs carried on great wooden pillars, the way halls were raised on that island. There's a story people tell in Demak about one of those pillars, said to be pieced together from leftover wood chips by a saintly teacher. It's a story, not a record, but it shows how dearly the building is loved. The Qur'an says God made people "nations and tribes that ye may know one another." The mosques look like their nations. The rows inside look the same.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · `MUD IN MALI, FROM THE RIVER.` · `TIMBER AND CURVED ROOFS IN CHINA.` · `TIERED ROOFS ON PILLARS IN JAVA.` · then, large: `NATIONS AND TRIBES THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: build a mosque in your mind out of what's around you. Settle, and breathe. Look at the room you're in, or remember the place you grew up. What would a house of prayer be made of there? Brick, stone, timber, glass, adobe, the gray concrete of a city block? What would keep it cool, or warm? Where would the light come in? Let it take shape slowly, wall by wall. Last of all, choose one wall and give it a small mark for the direction of prayer. That mark is the one thing every mosque shares. If you pray, you can bring that house into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Djenné, the Malian town whose mud mosque has thick walls for the heat and wooden poles that give plasterers a foothold when it's renewed. Today's word.
Your line: every land builds its own. Today, look up one mosque that surprises you, a roof or a wall you'd never have guessed, and notice what it's made of. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims pray in mosques of every style and material, and when no mosque is near they pray on any clean ground or a prayer mat, facing the direction of Mecca.
